docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Introduction to GITHUB

These notes are provided to give you a starting point with learning GITHUB. In a previous exercise, we created a GIT repository (repo); this provides a repo on one computer only, usable for one user. This is a local version control system, with a local repo. But we could keep a GIT repo on many different computers, or perhaps on a file share. This would be normal practice when developing closed source.

GITHUB uses GIT and allows us to create a repo in the cloud where we can store a repository. It’s just another computer in the cloud, running GIT. Once a repo is there, we can clone a repo to any other computer and as we make changes, we can push them to the GITHUB repo. Now we can share code with other users as well.

But we have much more here; we have user management and many integrated tools.

As always, we have the churn and instability of commercial IT. By the time I have written these notes, they will be out of date, and the GUI will have changed. The best I can hope for it to create examples that work, such that you can figure out how to replicate, even when the GUI changes.

docs.title: Web Setup
docs.text:
One of the disciplines we need to get right, is to be able to follow a brief exactly.

Go to GITHUB.com and create an account. Call it L12345678, where the name is your L number. You will use this to submit some of your continuous assessment (CA).

You may create a personal account as well, but that is nothing to do with this programme of study.

As a student, you are entitled to a student toolkit and its FREE!

You will need to verify your student account, there will be a CAPTCHA or similar test.

You also need to verify using your e-mail address.

Go through the hello-world activity and understand GITHUB's terminology.

Many people create public repos, you can now search on any topic you are interested in. If you find a project you are interested in, you can watch, so you are updated when changes occur.

There is a marketplace, you can search this for commercial tools to improve your development work.

Add an avatar/picture; be polite!

Note that everyone can now see this repo, do not create assignments here unless you secure them as private. Mark all the repos you create here as Private.

Create a private repo called First

There are some options:

  • Visibility Private
  • No template
  • Add a README file (Yes)
  • Add a .gitignore for Python files
  • Use the MIT license

Then click Create new repository

Fig 1. New repo settings.

Review what has been created, examine the files to review their contents. You will now see a standard interface; mine is show below.

Fig 2. Repo.

docs.title: readme.md
docs.text:
Edit the readme.md file as you go along, someone browsing your repo should be able to understand the repo fully based on what is written here. Typical practice is to have headings on:

  • Objective of the project, what problem the project will address.
  • How users can get started with the project, dependencies, environment.
  • Where users can get help with the project.
  • Who maintains and contributes to the project. Do not post e-mail addresses.
  • If there is major documentation in sections, you could link to it from here.
  • If its complicated, include a table of contents with links.

readme.md should be short, its a summary, not detail. I am not a fan of badges, etc. but feel free to add.

docs.title: GITHUB on Windows
docs.text: I mostly do code development in Linux, but I'll run through some Windows examples here.

docs.title: Security Changes
docs.text: There was a change made to the way security works a few versions of GitHub back. I do not want to get into SSH keys, Tokens etc. for now. When you are installing GitHub, install Credentials Manager, it is one of the final options. When you are authenticating to a repo, this will prompt you for credentials via the web browser. Make a mental note: down the line, you will be using SSH keys for most of your sync with GitHub, but there is only so much we can pack in for now.

docs.title: Cloning a repo
docs.text:
The computer I'm using for this exercise has the unwieldy path to my GITHUB files of C:\Users\John ORaw\OneDrive\GITHUB.johnoraw-education

cd C:\Users\John ORaw\OneDrive\GITHUB.johnoraw-education

I am going to clone the repo called First.

git clone https://github.com/JOR-Donegal/First.git

This creates a new directory called First with the files I previously had in GitHub.

Fig 3. Cloning.

docs.title: Adding a local file In Windows
docs.text:
I add a text file (jor.txt) with some random text. Can you figure out the old DOS command copy con?

Fig 4. Create a test file.

I add this for staging and then commit the new file. You should know what all this means from the previous notes.

Fig 5. Stage and Commit.

But the message "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit."??

docs.title: Checking the remote origin
docs.text:
Because I originally cloned from a remote origin, Git knows where I can fetch or push things to. In Git, an origin is a pointer to the URL where you copied the repo from. Origin is the default remote name in Git. I should check all my configuration.

Fig 6. Config.

The config includes details of where this repo was copied from, the origin.

docs.title: Pushing to the remote origin
docs.text:
I have a new file committed which is not in the remote location. I can now push this.

Fig 7. Pushing my changes back.

And then check through the web browser to see if this worked.

Fig 8. Verify the changes.

docs.title: Pulling from remote
docs.text:
I only update in one place at a time, once we have conflicting updates in two different places, the world gets complicated.

Through my web browser, I click on jor.txt

Fig 9. Online file.

I click on the pen symbol to edit.

Fig 10. Online edit.

I make a meaningless edit (!) and Commit the change. Note that I need to give a message for the commit.

Fig 11. Online commit.

On my local computer I can know see this change and pull it.

Fig 12. Pull.

Finally, I verify the history of changes to that file.

Fig 13. Pull.

docs.title: Repo from local files
docs.text:
Sometimes I populate a repo from local files.

Using the web interface, create a new empty public repo called Second

Fig 14. New Repo.

At setup I can see the URL as https://github.com/JOR-Donegal/Second.git

On the next page, I have several options, but I do nothing else here.

Fig 15. Landing page.

On my local PC, I create a new folder called Second and create some directories in it. Then I copy some random files to the directories. I called my directories rubbish 1-4, I left directory 4 empty, no files.

Fig 16. Dummy directories.

Open a terminal at this path.

I use git status to see if this is already a repo. I then ran commands to make it a repo.

Fig 17. Commands to create a repo.

In Fig 15, some commands were recommended to push a repo from the command line, I will use these now.

Fig 18. Push a repo.

If we review the repo, it looks almost correct. There is no folder called rubbish4. Can you figure out why?

Fig 19. Push a repo.

Note the command git add * and identify what is does. Any directory which was empty did not copy up!

docs.title: Integrate VSCode
docs.text:
Everything I’m doing here uses Git, but also ties into GitHub. I am always reluctant to do walkthroughs with a GUI, as interfaces change so regularly. As long as you can follow the logic we are good. You can figure out any changes in the interface as you carry out these exercises.

I open Visual Studio Code and select a folder which has an existing repo cloned from GitHub (Second).

I sign in and open a terminal window to Output.

I make a small edit to a file and click Save. The filename changes color, signalling that it has been changed.

Fig 20. Change a file.

I click on Source Control, and I can see the changed file.

Fig 21. Source Control.

I have options to discard (curvy arrow) or add (+), hover over them to distinguish.

If I add, I can see a new tab, Staged Changes.

Fig 22. Staged changes.

If I click on the Commit dropdown I can see the Git commands. I select Commit

Visual studio asks for a message to accompany the change.

Fig 23. Comments.

I then click the Commit button. My local Git repo is now clean, but is one revision ahead of the origin, my GitHub repo. I can now Sync changes. But first, I select the Output screen of the terminal and select to show GIT.

Fig 24. Synch.

If I monitor the output, I can see the detail of the push to the repo.

Fig 25. GIT log.

And I can verify on GitHub.

Fig 26. Verification.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: I am not going to do a detailed walkthrough here. GIT commands are the same and when I cover using Linux, it should all make sense. You may come back to these notes in a few weeks.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Usernames and passwords are old fashioned and low security. It's much better to use SSH keys and logging on and off from Linux servers.

On a Linux server called Sonar1 or any Linux IoT device, I create a unique SSH key.

''''linux ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "john.oraw@hotmail.com" ''''

I check the ~/.ssh directory

Fig 27. SSH Directory.

Did I make a mistake...you can see my public key?

Do you notice, I didn't show you my private key?

Think about it!

docs.title: GITHUB
docs.text:
On GITHUB, I go to my personal profile and add the SSH key, with a meaningful name. I'm currently working on an IoT device called sonar1 running Raspbian OS. Eventually, this IoT device will control a transducer on a robotic vessel.

I check to see if everything is working.

Fig 28. Verification.

docs.title: GH Command Line
docs.text:
Some time ago, the ability to authenticate at the command line with a username and password, was deprecated. If you are using a system with a web browser, you can use it to authenticate and obtain a token.

From c. 2019, for work at the command, the GH CLI tool began to emerge.

Take a look here and install on a server/headless system.

docs.title: Forks
docs.text:
A GitHub fork is unique to GitHub, it does not exist in Git. Whenever someone creates a public repository, you can copy it over to your own account. This is one of the huge advantages of GitHub. After you fork, there is no link between the two, you will not get any future updates from the original repo.

Sometimes we copy an entire repo to our own account. In this example, I am working with two repos that I have. I have already created some material on one of them.

Fig 29. Two repos.

In the JohnORaw repo, I can search for the repo I want to copy using the search bar.

Fig 30. Two repos.

If I click on this, I can see the public repository. There is a fork button.

Fig 31. Fork button.

If I click the fork button, an exact copy of this repo is made to my JohnORaw GitHub account, at this point in time.

Fig 32. Fork copy.

Everything was copied. Examine the commits which have been made.

Fig 33. Fork copy.

This shows me the commit history (these screenshots from November 2022).

Fig 34. History.

The original repo could have reverted to earlier versions and earlier commits, so can I in the forked repo. I can see the hash associated with each version.

I may have only had read/public access to the original repo, I could not have made changes. But once I clone the repo, its mine, I have full rights to make changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Work with another student in the class and fork one of their public repos.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
In previous notes we looked at the git log command. We saw that each commit has a long SHA256 code associated with it.

Fig 35. Logs.

We saw the HEAD keyword, pointing at the most recent commit that the repo has a record of. Instead of using the long SHA256 code, we can just use the keyword HEAD. I can look in detail at the most recent change.

Fig 36. Show an edit.

Remember, red for deleted, green for new. I can see the same information in GitHub, the SHA keys are shortened to the first 7 characters.

Fig 37. View Commit.

If I click on the SHA code, I can view the commit. The information should be consistent with what I saw using git log through the terminal.

Fig 38. Confirm in GITHUB.

docs.title: Undo before Staging
docs.text:
My starting point is to check the current status, both locally and in VSCode.

Fig 39. GIT status .

Now I’m making a small change in jor.txt and saving but I have not staged or committed.

Fig 40. GIT status . Fig 41. Diff .

Imagine I have broken something, and I want to revert to the last committed version. If I use the command git checkout filename I can revert to the previous version. I could also use git restore filename.

Fig 42. Checkout .

docs.title: Undo after Staging
docs.text:
I have changed the same file again and this time, I have staged the change.

Fig 43. Status.

You may notice, each time git tells me my options! In this case, I will restore the staged file.

Fig 44. Status.

Now I can either remodify or restore from the last commit.

docs.title: Undo after Commit
docs.text:
This time I will stage and commit all using VSCode. I am using the message “Update at 14:46”.

Fig 45. Status.

First, I need to identify the version I want. As you can see, my messages are very unhelpful, that is a lesson! I want to revert to a previous saved version.

Fig 46. Log.

To go back to that version, I can also use git checkout hash with the hash of the version I want to restore.

Fig 47. Roll back.

I can then commit this and push it to GitHub.

Fig 48. Commit.

And finally, to check it really has updated....

Fig 49. Verify.

docs.title: New projects
docs.text:
Where we have complex projects with multiple developers, we need some way to allow users to work independently. And once we have a usable project, we will need to add features from time to time. We alo have to maintain the project, with bug and security fixes.

In GIT, we can work on multiple branches of a project simultaneously without breaking the main project.

I created a new repo called BranchTest on GitHub. I created a directory OneDrive - Atlantic TU\GitHub\BranchTest and created a single batch file in the directory, setup.cmd.

echo "# BranchTest" >> README.md
git init
git add README.md
git commit -m "first commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/GreatlyImprovedTechnology/BranchTest.git
git push -u origin main

My file setup.cmd is not in the GitHub repo, in this case, I’ll add it and I check online to confirm.

Fig 50. Create new repo.

The question arises, should I have included this file in the repo, or should I have excluded any such local build files in a .gitignore file? And as for my readme.md, GitHub kept the quote marks and didn’t render the line as markdown. I edited the line in GitHub and did a pull to resync.

Fig 51. Pull.

That renders properly now!

Fig 52. Verify.

docs.title: Local
docs.text:
I am going to create my branch architecture locally. I am up to date and on the branch called main.

Fig 53. Check status.

I have already made a few changes.

Fig 54. Check status.

I can create a new branch and then check to see what branches exist. I can see I have two branches, and the * symbol tells me which branch I have currently selected as active.

Fig 55. New branch, dev.

If I create a new branch, it should include those commits. To change branches, I use the checkout command.

Fig 56. Checkout.

Notice that HEAD is now pointing to Dev.

docs.title: Feature Branch
docs.text:
As discussed in the theory notes, we should be doing commits on code changes on dedicated feature branches. When they are looking good, we can merge them to dev or test. I am going to add initial pages to my repo. This time, I’m going to use an option -b to create and change branches in a single command.

Fig 57. Checkout.

And I verify I am on the right branch.

Fig 58. Verify branch.

Next, I add in some files, and test them to ensure they basically work. After, I check where I am with git status.

Fig 59. Verify status.

I stage and commit these files to the initial_pages branch.

If I have done something stupid and broken the application, it doesn’t matter! The permanent branches, main, test and dev do not utilize this new code, it is only on the specific feature branch.

Fig 60. Commit.

docs.title: Remote
docs.text:
I could create my branch architecture on GitHub. In the previous exercises, I didn’t do a push, so I can see right now that I have only a single branch on GitHub.

Fig 61. Review GITHUB.

To create a branch test from Main, I make sure Main is selected and the enter my new branch name.

Fig 62. Create a branch.

I’m going to create a branch as if I was doing a bug-fix. I create a branch from Test called bug-fix-readme and I make a trivial edit so I can track the change.

Fig 63. Make a change.

I commit the change. If I change to the Test or main branch, this change will not appear. Check that in your own exercise to verify.

docs.title: Merging locally
docs.text:
On my local machine, I will merging the changes from GitHub, I pull changes from remote.

Fig 64. Pull from remote.

I can pull the remote Test branch.

Fig 65. Pull from Test.

And I also pull the bug-fix-readme branch.

Fig 66. Pull from Test.

If I do a git log command, I can see my trivial edit!

Fig 67. GIT log.

Now I can merge the bug fix back into Test. I make Test active and merge the bug fix branch into it. I can then delete my bug fix branch both locally and remotely.

Fig 68. Merge.

I check on GitHub and although the bug-fix-readme branch is gone, the Test branch has not been updated. I need to Push it.

Fig 69. Push.

I check on GitHub, the change is there!

Fig 70. Verify.

docs.title: Merging changes to GitHub
docs.text:
In this exercise, I will merge the changes from my local machine to GitHub. I still have a branch called dev on my local machine that does not show on GitHub.

I can git checkout dev to switch to that branch, but if I try to push, there is no upstream branch to push to. However, I can force this.

Fig 71. Checkout dev.

Checking on GitHub, my branch is there.

Fig 72. Verify.

I can see the commits, but earlier I created an initial_pages branch from dev and I did not merge it. On my local machine, I switch to dev and merge initial_pages.

Fig 73. Merge.

And I can verify this worked.

Fig 74. Verify.

Remember to tidy up!

Fig 75. Verify.

We didn’t sync this branch to GitHub, so that should be all traces gone.

docs.title: Final sync
docs.text:
I now have three branches which have different status. If I go back to Code and select branches, I can see that Test and dev are 1 commit ahead of main. Hover your mouse above the numbers to clarify this.

Fig 76. Review on GITHUB.

We sync the branches using pull requests. We do this manually and we must accept the changes. If I click on New pull request, I see a summary of the changes. Off screen (it is too big to show!) I see a description of all five files.

Fig 77. Summary.

I click to Create pull request. I now have the opportunity to approve this request. If this was a multi-programmer project, this sort of workflow would be critical.

Fig 78. Pull request.

I click to merge pull request and then to confirm. I can see this was successful.

Fig 79. Verify pull request.

And when I go back to check the main branch, my files are there.

Fig 80. Verify main.

docs.title: Finally
docs.text:
Using GitHub simply becomes second nature after a little while. Start by being methodical. Write a CHEAT SHEET for commands to do things and verify that it all works. When you need to revert to a previous version, you should be able to use your CHEAT SHEET. If I do not use these tools for a few months, I need my CHEAT SHEET! When I'm doing a development project, after a day, I'm fine again.

We have all developed practices in version control, and if you find any good, authoritative guides, please send them on to me!

When I'm coding, I'm doing one job at a time. Suppose in an assignment, I am adding code to check for previously discovered network addresses. At the start of my work, I'll make sure I have a clean repo. I make a change to main.py and I create a function in a separate file. I check that this works, and they do a commit with a meaningful message stating what I've done. I've changed two files, and neither change would make sense by itself. The commit is atomic in nature and encapsulates the entire change.

If I spend more than 30 minutes without a commit, I'm probably breaking my work up into chunks that are too big.

As always, my notes are out of date by the time I've written them. An added problem, how much can I cover in the available time where students have never worked with GIT/GITHUB etc. before. Next steps, do the GitHub foundations course, it's free and it will look good on your CV. And it will also be more current than my notes.

At the GitHub skills site, run through the first week on GitHub exercises. You will use markdown throughout this course of study. On completion, you should understand the basics and also, how to use markdown.

Apologies for Mona the cat!
